=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer-side assessment

The Seller’s package is not balanced against Wattlebridge’s stated deal: 100% of Paperbark Analytics for AUD 24 million, debt-free/cash-free, under NSW law. Several positions would leave the Buyer paying the agreed price while inheriting known liabilities, uncertain title to important IP, or transaction risks with little effective recourse. The Disclosure Letter also tries to make broad disclosure do more work than its specific entries support.

This review is based on the Seller materials provided, not the complete SPA or due diligence record. The final drafting should be checked against both.

## Material pushbacks

### 1. Liability caps, thresholds and time limits

- **General cap of AUD 4.8 million (20% of price):** This is a substantial reduction in recourse. Push for a higher general cap, with separate treatment for specific indemnities and identified risks. The cap should not apply to fraud, deliberate concealment or other agreed carve-outs.
- **AUD 25,000 de minimis and AUD 250,000 tipping/excess basket:** These thresholds could leave numerous smaller losses unrecoverable, and the excess-only basket means the Seller pays nothing for the first AUD 250,000. Seek a lower de minimis and a **tipping basket** (once crossed, the full amount is recoverable), or delete the basket for specific indemnities and known matters.
- **18-month general warranty claim period:** This may be too short to discover and quantify latent matters. Seek a longer period, with appropriate longer periods for tax and other claims that may emerge later.
- **“Any limitation … applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise”:** Reject this default. The SPA should state expressly which limits apply to which claims; silence should not extend general warranty limits to indemnities, purchase-price adjustments, debt/cash claims, fraud, or other separately agreed remedies.
- **Fundamental/title warranties under the general regime:** Reject. Capacity, authority and title to the shares go to whether the Buyer receives what it is buying. Seek a separate, materially higher cap—potentially up to the purchase price—and a longer claim period, subject to negotiation. The DD-012 share register is evidence of the recorded holder, not a substitute for warranties and completion deliverables establishing good title, fully paid shares and absence of encumbrances.

### 2. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance

The Seller says the limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to **all Claims of any nature**. That could curtail remedies beyond ordinary warranty claims, including specific indemnities and other contractual rights. It also risks making general drafting override protections negotiated for particular matters.

Limit these provisions to the claims they are intended to govern. Preserve the operation of specific indemnities and other express remedies, and carve out fraud and deliberate concealment. Review the complete SPA carefully: the effect depends on the actual interaction between clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5.

### 3. Data-room and public-register disclosure; Buyer knowledge

- **General disclosure of DD-002 to DD-012, the Accounts, registers and public records:** Reject blanket disclosure. It makes it difficult to know which facts qualify which warranties and shifts the burden of interpreting a large data room to the Buyer. Require specific, fair disclosure against the relevant warranty, with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter. The specific entries in this letter themselves acknowledge important gaps.
- **Knowledge exclusion covering the Buyer and advisers, including discoverable matters:** Reject. It could remove claims because information was in a data room or publicly searchable, even if it was not actually known or appreciated. At most, any knowledge qualifier should be tightly defined by actual knowledge of named individuals after reasonable enquiry; mere discoverability should not count. Do not let diligence findings silently waive contractual protections.

### 4. Known matters need tailored treatment—not just disclosure

**Bluefen — consent is not yet evidenced.** The customer represents about AUD 3.6 million, or 30%, of FY26 revenue. The Seller acknowledges no final written consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied. “Reasonable endeavours” is not enough if consent is important to the transaction, and treating it as satisfied upon delivery of a written consent could ignore unsatisfied conditions. Require a condition precedent to Completion: final, unconditional consent and evidence that all relevant conditions have been satisfied or waived. Include a termination right if it is not obtained by the long-stop date; do not complete on an incomplete consent.

**Riverlark — AUD 3.2 million facility and security remain outstanding.** A release only after Completion is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free purchase and leaves the Buyer exposed to repayment and security-release risk. Require repayment or agreed discharge through the Completion funds flow, with lender payout and executed releases delivered at Completion. Confirm the treatment of accrued interest, fees and any other debt-like items.

**Ironquay — IP ownership/transfer is unresolved.** Under DD-004, transfer of SOW3 Project Materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee; DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open, with no payment receipt or confirmatory assignment. The existing indemnity, limited to a specific SOW3 payment, does not establish that the Company owns or can use the materials, and may not cover the wider consequences of missing rights. Require evidence of cleared payment and an effective assignment (or other legally sufficient rights) by Completion, plus appropriate IP warranties and a tailored indemnity if needed. Do not treat the Seller’s statement that the current indemnity is “adequate” as resolving the issue.

**DD-005 — AUD 420,000 conditional bonuses omitted from funds flow.** These are a material, known Completion-linked liability, with possible payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs not addressed. Require them and all associated on-costs to be included in the Completion accounts/funds flow and treated consistently with the agreed debt-free/cash-free and price mechanics. The Seller should fund or bear any agreed pre-Completion liability; avoid paying for the business as if those obligations do not exist and then inheriting them.

**DD-006 — export/privacy incident remains preliminary.** The data may involve about 1,240 records, and access, scope and notification obligations remain unknown. Calling it “not expected to be material” is not a resolution. Require updated investigation results and relevant records before Completion, appropriate privacy/data-security warranties, and a specific indemnity or other tailored allocation for losses and remediation costs attributable to the incident. Consider a condition or special remedy if the investigation reveals material exposure. Do not assert a confirmed breach on the current disclosure.

**Supplier renewals — AUD 330,000 aggregate.** The Seller calls these ordinary-course costs, but the letter does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or outside ordinary-course commitments. Require contract-level detail and confirmation of status, termination rights, payment obligations and any prepayments or arrears. Ensure they are treated consistently in Completion accounts and working capital; do not accept a conclusory “ordinary-course” label.

### 5. Other disclosures and conditions

- **Office lease:** The letter identifies a notification obligation, not a share-sale consent requirement. Require the actual lease provision and evidence of compliance with any notice obligation; do not assume consent is required, but do not leave notice compliance unaddressed.
- **Mossvale:** The restriction concerns assignment and does not say consent is required merely because shares are sold. Check the actual clause and transaction structure; seek confirmation that the share sale does not trigger a consent or other breach rather than accepting an unsupported assumption either way.
- **Tax and IP warranties:** The Seller says these are “settled” under the general regime, but supplies no substantive terms establishing that. Seek meaningful tax and IP warranties and appropriate separate caps, periods and remedies. The complete SPA and tax diligence are needed to calibrate them.
- **Title:** DD-012 records Harbourglass as registered holder. Require the Seller’s express title warranties and delivery at Completion of properly executed transfer documents, updated registers and evidence of good title, free of encumbrances. The register is a source document, not a waiver of the Seller’s obligations.

## Recommended negotiating position

1. Reject the blanket regime applying general caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive-remedy provisions and non-reliance language to every claim. Define their scope expressly and preserve agreed exceptions and separate remedies.
2. Seek stronger, separately negotiated protection for title/fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities and known risks; remove or narrow the de minimis, basket and general-disclosure provisions.
3. Make Bluefen consent and the Riverlark repayment/security release deliverable Completion requirements, not post-Completion hopes.
4. Resolve Ironquay rights, bonus liabilities and the incident through evidence, funds-flow treatment, tailored warranties/indemnities and, where appropriate, a Completion condition.
5. Replace data-room/public-record and discoverability-based disclosure or knowledge exclusions with specific, fair disclosure and a narrow actual-knowledge standard.
6. Obtain the complete SPA, relevant underlying contracts and updated diligence before finalising the mark-up—especially for the Bluefen consent conditions, Riverlark discharge mechanics, Ironquay SOW3 rights, incident investigation and the price-adjustment definitions.
